$comment: DSH adaptation layer. The vendored tree under skills/ stays a byte-for-byte copy of upstream;
everything in this file is applied in memory by the skill provider, so `vendor-skills.mjs --check`
can still prove the baseline is pristine. Each rule is an exact literal find/replace plus the
number of occurrences the rule expects: a count mismatch fails the drift check instead of
silently half-applying after an upstream reword.
Why these edits exist: upstream is written for Claude Code, where `/name` is a command the model
can run. In DSH `/name` is a user-facing slash command, and a skill marked
`disable-model-invocation: true` cannot be loaded by the model at all, so the routing prose has to
name skills instead of issuing commands. See skills/dsh-workflow/ for the model-facing contract.

rules.note: blocker: the original opening promises Claude Code hooks that DSH does not run; lead with the DSH reality
rules.find:
# Setup Git Guardrails

Sets up a PreToolUse hook that intercepts and blocks dangerous git commands before Claude executes them.
rules.replace:
# Setup Git Guardrails (Claude Code hooks — not active in DSH)

> **DSH users: do not follow this skill as written.** It installs a Claude Code `PreToolUse` hook into `.claude/settings.json` or `~/.claude/settings.json`. DeepSeek Harness does not read those files, so the guardrail would never fire and the user would believe they were protected when they are not.
>
> DSH has no settings-file hook layer at all — its protections are the filesystem sandbox / approval policy (the permission presets and `sandbox_permissions`) and, for git specifically, hooks the *repo* enforces. If the user asks for git guardrails in DSH:
> 1. Say plainly that this skill targets Claude Code and is inactive here.
> 2. Offer the DSH-native substitutes: a `pre-commit`/`pre-push` git hook in the repo, installed by the repo so it fires no matter which harness is driving (`setup-pre-commit` covers the pre-commit half), or an approval/sandbox policy the user sets in DSH.
> 3. Only if the user also drives Claude Code in this repo, continue below to install the hook for that harness.

The rest of this file is the original Claude Code procedure: it sets up a `PreToolUse` hook that intercepts and blocks dangerous git commands before the agent executes them.

rules.note: blocker: the whole point of this skill is Claude Code's background CLI; DSH delegates in-process
rules.find: Write a handoff summary of the current conversation so a fresh agent can continue the work. Instead of saving it, launch a background agent seeded with the summary as its prompt: `claude --bg --name "<descriptive name>" "<handoff summary>"`. It starts in the current working directory and returns immediately; the user manages it with `claude agents`.
rules.replace: Write a handoff summary of the current conversation so a fresh agent can continue the work. In DSH you do not shell out to another CLI for this: delegate with the `subagent` tool, passing the summary as the prompt (it runs in this workspace and returns its own report), or `subagent_fork` when the child should inherit this conversation instead of just the summary. Both return a durable agent id immediately, so keep working and pick the result up later with `job_output`/`list_agents` and `send_message`.

rules.replace: Give the delegation a descriptive `description` (DSH shows it as the child's label in the subagent list) — that replaces the CLI's `--name`, and there is no job list or terminal title to set.

rules.note: the summary becomes a subagent prompt, and the suggested skills must respect DSH's invocation gate
rules.find: Include a "suggested skills" section in the summary, which suggests skills that the agent should invoke.
rules.replace: Include a "suggested skills" section in the summary. Name only skills the child can actually load — in DSH the `skill` tool rejects anything marked `disable-model-invocation: true`, so list those as "the user runs this one" instead of instructing the child to load them.
